harf-e-zaid.title: حرف زائد
harf-e-zaid.caption: Harf-e-zaid, the redundant letter, discussed at length
harf-e-zaid.description: Hamza and Zoya open with a contract in which a clause says 'no' and the lawyer calmly reads it as 'I swear', the kind of surplus word no one would accept in a legal document, let alone a revealed one. That is harf-e-zaid, the redundant letter, and against the grammarians' habit of calling a letter surplus stands Hazrat Mahdi ahs's ruling that the Quran holds not one. With Mughni al-Labib they follow a single 'min' through its work of naming a kind, taking a part, explaining and giving a cause; hear the 'la' before the oath on the city as the answer to a denial the deniers had not yet voiced; find the taunt of madness in one surah answered in another, because the whole Quran is one surah; watch a later master refute two great grammarians who had called a second 'la' surplus; and see 'lata' turn out to be one complete verb rather than 'la' with a letter tacked on. They close by asking whether we dismiss as filler the hesitations of the people around us, and what we miss when we do.

harf-e-zaid.title: حرف زائد
harf-e-zaid.caption: Harf-e-zaid, the redundant letter, from Noor e Imaan
harf-e-zaid.description: Hamza and Zoya take the short road through harf-e-zaid, the redundant letter: whether a book as perfect as the Quran can carry the filler words our own writing leans on. With Mughni al-Labib and the sayings of Hazrat Mahdi ahs they read the 'min' of Surah Fatir as a spotlight on the kind of mercy meant rather than a loose joint, the 'la' before the oath of Surah al-Balad as a refusal of the deniers' claims before the oath is sworn, since the whole Quran reads as one surah, and 'lata' as a complete verb with no letter to spare. They end by asking what treasures a reader walks past in daily recitation.

thumbnail.title: Kya Quran mein koi *harf zaid* hai?

hazf.title: حذف
hazf.caption: Hazf, ellipsis, from Noor e Imaan

hazf.title: حذف
hazf.caption: Hazf, ellipsis, discussed at length
hazf.description: Hamza and Zoya start from a text message that says only 'got home', which its reader understands whole, and carry that into hazf, ellipsis: the commentators' theory that words are missing from the Quran at many places, counted by one grammarian in forty-six kinds. Against it stands Hazrat Mahdi ahs's ruling that the Quran has no hazf: a word the context supplies is muqaddar, present in the hearer's mind, and manwi, intended by the speaker, not absent. They ask how rules of rhetoric compiled centuries after the revelation came to judge it, like a tailor who trims the customer to fit the coat, and set itnab, saying much, against ijaz, the brevity that is Arabic eloquence at its height. Then three verses: in Surah al-Hadid, how 'not equal' already calls for the second party, which the next line names; in Surah al-Baqarah, how the springs gushing from the rock tell us Hazrat Musa as struck it without a word for the blow, like an engine answering a turned key; and in Surah al-Hajj, how 'it is the piety of hearts' loses its force once two words are added. They close by asking whether we too misread what does not fit the moulds of our own making.

istisna-munqati.title: استثناء منقطع
istisna-munqati.caption: Istisna munqati, the disjoined exception, a brief overview

istisna-munqati.title: استثناء منقطع
istisna-munqati.caption: Istisna munqati, the disjoined exception, discussed at length
istisna-munqati.description: Hamza and Zoya take the long way through istisna munqati, the exception that seems to cut away from what came before. They begin with the two kinds of exception, then follow Hazrat Mahdi ahs's position that the Quran holds no disjoined exception into two verses the grammarians had given up on: in Surah Yunus, how the township and the people of Yunus turn out to be one and the same, and in Surah al-Baqarah, how amani means recitation or invented tales rather than wishes. They end with what the principle asks of a reader of people as well as of books.

jumla-e-mustanifa.title: جملہ مستأنفہ
jumla-e-mustanifa.caption: Jumla-e-mustanifa, the resumptive clause, from Noor e Imaan

jumla-e-mustanifa.title: جملہ مستأنفہ
jumla-e-mustanifa.caption: Jumla-e-mustanifa, the resumptive clause, discussed at length
jumla-e-mustanifa.description: Hamza and Zoya ask whether one small point of grammar, whether a sentence joins the one before it or breaks away, can change the meaning of a revealed book. They picture jumla-e-mustanifa, the resumptive clause, as a train whose coupling has been pulled, and trace how commentators applying rules written after the revelation declared a fresh sentence wherever their rules found no join. Against that stands Hazrat Mahdi ahs's position that the Quran holds no such clause at all. They test it on two verses: in Surah Aal-e-Imran, how those firmly grounded in knowledge share the knowledge of ta'wil with Allah rather than beginning a new sentence, with Hazrat Mujahid rh and Hazrat Ibn Abbas rz as witnesses and a chain of knowledge running from the Prophet slm; and in Surah al-A'raf, how the men on the heights who have not yet entered the garden are described by that clause, not cut off from it. They close wondering how many more such secrets wait behind the veil of grammar.

jumla-e-mutarida.title: جملۂ معترضہ
jumla-e-mutarida.caption: Jumla-e-mutarida, the parenthetical clause, discussed at length
jumla-e-mutarida.description: Hamza and Zoya open with the source code of the universe, where no bracket is spare, and carry that image into jumla-e-mutarida, the parenthetical clause the grammarians read as a remark dropped into a sentence. They set out Hazrat Mahdi ahs's position that the Quran holds no such clause, and test it on three verses the commentators had bracketed: in Surah al-Baqarah, how the warning that makes no difference to the deniers is the first of two predicates, not an aside; further on, how the Israelites' insha Allah is a condition with its answer rather than a pious tag; and in Surah al-A'raf, how the promise that no soul is burdened beyond its capacity is the predicate itself, in the state of raf'. They close by asking whether the seemingly stray moments of a life are parenthetical either.

jumla-e-mutarida.title: جملۂ معترضہ
jumla-e-mutarida.caption: Jumla-e-mutarida, the parenthetical clause, from Noor e Imaan
jumla-e-mutarida.description: Hamza and Zoya take the short road through jumla-e-mutarida, the parenthetical clause: a remark dropped into a sentence, like a blessing slipped into a jurist's reported ruling, which can be lifted out without touching the ruling itself. The commentators admitted such clauses in the Quran; Hazrat Mahdi ahs's position is that it holds none, every line bearing weight like a beam in a building's plan. Three verses carry the proof: in Surah al-Baqarah, 'alike to them whether you warn them' is the first predicate, not an aside; the Israelites' insha Allah is a condition on what follows, not a pious tag; and in Surah al-A'raf, 'We burden no soul beyond its capacity' is the argument for what precedes it. They end by asking whether our own everyday words carry connections we habitually ignore.

naskh.title: نسخ
naskh.caption: Naskh, abrogation, discussed at length
naskh.description: Hamza and Zoya begin with a phone whose update is said to have left half its features obsolete, until the software's maker explains that nothing was removed and each feature has its own moment. That is naskh, abrogation, as they take it up: Shah Waliullah Dehlavi rh's al-Fawz al-Kabir records that five hundred verses were once held abrogated, a count he cut to five, and against even those five stands Hazrat Mahdi ahs's ruling that no verse of the Quran is abrogated. They test each: the bequest verse of Surah al-Baqarah, which fills the gap inheritance leaves for relatives who cannot inherit; the twenty against two hundred of Surah al-Anfal, eased to a hundred as a concession while the standard stands; the wives verses of Surah al-Ahzab, where the supposed abrogating verse came down earlier and only draws a limit; the charity before private counsel in Surah al-Mujadila, a filter that Hazrat Ali rz alone acted on and whose spirit lives in zakat; and the night vigil of Surah al-Muzzammil, laid on the Prophet slm alone and eased for the companions who followed him into it. They close by asking which commands we have quietly abrogated for ourselves out of convenience.
